subject: Private deployment connection model decision: PrivateLink vs peering vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Jessica Park <jessica.park@fidelity-consult.com>
To: jonas.weber@redwood.com
Cc: Peter Murray <peter.murray@finbridge.com>
Date: Tue, 30 Sep 2025 09:12:00 -07:00
Subject: Private deployment: connection model question (PrivateLink vs peering vs S2S VPN)

Hi Jonas,

Thanks for taking this — quick background: we (FinBridge) are planning to run Redwood Private inside our AWS tenant for a regulated lending product. Security/compliance is the primary constraint: no broad VPC routing, strict egress control, and auditability. We'll have two production VPCs (us-east-1 primary, eu-west-1 DR), some on-prem datacenter presence (legacy KVM farm), and a handful of shared services in a central tooling VPC (logging, auth).

Two immediate asks:
- From your experience, which connectivity mode minimizes our attack surface while preserving reasonable latency for user-facing requests (200 RPS typical, occasional bursts)?
- Any operational gotchas we should plan for (SNAT, source IP preservation, cross-account traffic billing, cross-region patterns)?

We're weighing: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or a site-to-site VPN. Budget for networking is moderate but not unlimited — prefer a solution that avoids heavy ongoing ops, but compliance trumps cost.

If you could share a short comparison (pros/cons + recommended default for production and fallback) and a high-level runbook for onboarding that would be great. Attaching a current network sketch.

Thanks,
Jessica Park
Principal Cloud Architect
Fidelity Consulting

Attachment: finbridge-network-sketch.pdf (attachment stub)

From: jonas_weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
To: Jessica Park <jessica.park@fidelity-consult.com>
Cc: Peter Murray <peter.murray@finbridge.com>, kimberly_park@redwood.com
Date: Tue, 30 Sep 2025 10:40:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment: connection model question (PrivateLink vs peering vs S2S VPN)

Jessica — thanks for the clear summary, this is a common pattern and we can make a pragmatic recommendation quickly. Short answer up front: PrivateLink-first for production control, peering for low-latency intra-account paths where full VPC routing is acceptable, and S2S VPN only for on-prem connectivity or as an emergency fallback.

Key rationale (high level):
- PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints)
  - Pros: minimal surface area (only the endpoint ENIs are reachable), works across accounts with VPC endpoint services, best for strictly limiting inbound paths, easier to audit connection acceptance.
  - Cons: slightly higher per-GB costs, targetable by per-endpoint security groups so more config items; cross-region requires additional endpoints or NLB fronting.

- VPC Peering
  - Pros: very low latency, low cost for intra-region transfer, transparent routing (no extra proxies).
  - Cons: broad routing by default unless you implement restrictive route tables and NACLs — increases blast radius; not transitive (need mesh for >2 VPCs).

- Site-to-Site VPN
  - Pros: works for on-prem and less complex to stand up for brownfield environments, can be an encrypted channel when you cannot use PrivateLink.
  - Cons: typically higher latency, less predictable throughput, brings the entire on-prem space into routing table considerations; operational-heavy for high-throughput.

Operational notes / gotchas to plan now:
- Source IP preservation: PrivateLink does not preserve client source IPs by default if you terminate at an NLB; we should decide whether preserving client IP in logs is required for your compliance.
- SNAT: If the Redwood Private node must call back into your shared VPC services, SNAT may be applied depending on the path — test path and flow logs early.
- Cross-account routing permissions: PrivateLink requires that the provider (us or your account) configure an endpoint-service; expect a short ownership verification step.
- Auditability: PrivateLink + VPC Flow Logs + CloudTrail gives the tightest, service-specific access logs.
- Cross-region: For your DR region we recommend standing up a second PrivateLink endpoint (or using global accelerator/NLB if you want a single FQDN).

Recommended immediate next steps:
1) Security review: confirm whether source-IP preservation is a blocker.
2) PoC: create a PrivateLink endpoint in your prod VPC pointing at our endpoint-service in us-east-1; test latency and tokenized traffic patterns.
3) Cost baseline: we'll run a quick estimate (I attached a baseline workbook).
4) Operational playbook: define fallback (peer or VPN) for scheduled failovers.

I've attached a concise comparison spreadsheet and a draft onboarding diagram. Happy to run a 30-min sync with your network/security engineers this week.

— Jonas
Jonas Weber
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Attachments: privatelink-peering-s2s-costs.xlsx, onboarding-draft-diagram.png

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Private deployment: connection model question (PrivateLink vs peering vs S2S VPN)

Thanks Jonas — a few operational items to flag for FinBridge before we lock to PrivateLink: 

- IP preservation detail: If you front with an NLB we see the client IP on the backend only when you enable proxy protocol or use target-group preservation; otherwise flows will look like the NLB ENI. If audit requires original client IP for throttling/forensics we should plan an architecture that preserves it (or capture it at the app layer).
- Egress and NAT: If Redwood instances in the customer's VPC need to call out to other AWS services in the same account, consider using route tables to force traffic via a central NAT or egress proxy. That helps with policy enforcement and vended egress logging.
- Cross-account billing: PrivateLink transfers are metered differently; include line items for endpoint hours and per-GB; peering is generally cheaper if the traffic volume is large and intra-region.
- Cross-region DR: PrivateLink across regions is not native — you'll need additional endpoints or an NLB in the DR region; peering across regions is possible via inter-region peering but has its own limits.

Operational recommendation: Primary = PrivateLink (prod), Secondary = intra-account peering for high-throughput batch jobs between your shared services and Redwood, Fallback = IPsec S2S VPN for on-prem connections and unexpected outages.

Ben — can you run a quick cost sensitivity (monthly) for 50/200/500 GB/day over PrivateLink vs peering and drop the numbers into our shared workbook?

Kimberly Park
Product Ops (Deployments), Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Private deployment: connection model question (PrivateLink vs peering vs S2S VPN)

Jessica — looping in the cost/ops side and attaching a more formal onboarding runbook and a finalized diagram. Quick summary of what we'll do if you approve:

1) Production onboarding (week 0–2):
   - Create PrivateLink endpoint in your prod VPCs and subscribe to Redwood's endpoint-service.
   - Enable VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail captures for the endpoint subnets.
   - Smoke test at low RPS; capture latency/99th percentile for 72 hours.
2) High-throughput paths (week 2–3):
   - If you have heavy intra-account data exchange (batch jobs), set up VPC peering between the shared-services VPC and the data-processing VPC — restrict routes to specific prefixes.
3) On-prem integration:
   - Set up an IPsec S2S VPN to the legacy KVM farm; limit routing to only the subnets required for token exchange.

Deliverables attached: mutual-action-plan.pdf and onboarding-diagram.png (diagram shows endpoint placement, route tables, and fallback flow). Please confirm if FinBridge legal needs to run any additional attestations for endpoint connections.

If it looks good I can kick off a scoped estimate and calendar the PoC this week.

Thanks — Ben
Ben Carter
Head of Customer Deployments, Redwood Inference
